To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
submicromolar doses of dopamine and dopamine agonists, acting at D2 receptors, increase the bandpass of retinal rod flicker responses.
dopamine, in concentrations that correspond to the endogenous retinal levels, biases the retinal circuits to increase the synaptic gain of cone over rod transmission to a second-order retinal neuron.
dopamine acts to increase the bandpass and the gain of the rod to horizontal cell transfer function.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of submicromolal levels of dopamine on the rod and cone inputs to second-order retinal neurons.
the mechanisms by which dopamine modulates the visual transduction cascade.
the role dopamine plays in the regulation of retinal function and its potential as an endogenous messenger in the visual system.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
dopamine, acting through D2 receptors, can modulate synaptic transfer from rods to horizontal cells and from rods to second order retinal neurons.
dopamine acts to bias the rod to horizontal cell circuit in favor of cone input.
dopamine acts as a modulator of rod and cone signals at the level of horizontal cell.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
dopamine acts as an intraretina messenger by biasing retinally mediated visual pathways to favor cone overrod inputs to higher order neurons.
dopamine is an important modulator of the retinal circuit that transmits rod and cone signals to the second-order neurons.
the effects of dopamine on retinal function are complex, and involve both D1 and D2 receptor subtypes.
The main takeaway from our work is that
dopamine can modulate the gain of rod to horizontal cell transmission.
the synaptic gains for rod and cone inputs to the second order retinal neurons are modifiable by dopamine and that the rod synaptic gain is altered in a manner that favors the cone signal.
endogenous dopamine can modulate the gain of rod transmission to second-order neurons.
